Do you have any of your wealth except what you have eaten and consumed?'"

Muslim and others narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, without mentioning the recitation of this surah or its revelation, with the wording: "The servant says: My wealth, my wealth. Of his wealth he has only three things: what he eats and consumes, what he wears and wears out, or what he gives in charity and preserves. Everything else is gone, and he leaves it to the people."

He said: "I will recite it to you a second time. Whoever weeps will have Paradise, and whoever cannot weep should feign weeping."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying: ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ means: the competition for more in wealth and children, boasting about their abundance, and vying with one another in them has preoccupied you.

It is said: *alhahu 'an kadha* (ألهاه عن كذا) and *alhahu* (ألهاه), meaning: when it occupied him. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*So I diverted her from the one with amulets, a suckling child.*

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of *alhakum* (ألهاكم) is: it made you forget.

﴿Until you visited the graves﴾ means: until death overtook you while you were in that state.

Qatadah said: the competition for more is boasting about tribes and clans.

Al-Dahhak said: *alhakum* means preoccupation with livelihood.

Muqatil and Qatadah also, and others, said: it was revealed concerning the Jews when they said, "We are more numerous than the sons of so-and-so, and the sons of so-and-so are more numerous than the sons of so-and-so." That preoccupied them until they died.

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning two clans of Quraysh: the Banu Abd Manaf and the Banu Sahm. They competed and vied in mastery and nobility in Islam. Each clan said: "We are more numerous in leadership, mightier in might, greater in men, and more numerous in commanders." The Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered the Banu Sahm, then they competed in the dead, and so the Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered them with their dead. So ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ was revealed, ﴿until you visited the graves﴾, boasting of the dead.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the Ansar.

*Al-Maqabir* (المقابر) is the plural of *maqbarah* (مقبرة), with the *ba'* vocalized either with a fatha or a damma.

The verse is evidence that preoccupation with worldly life, competing for more in it, and boasting in it are blameworthy traits. He, glory be to Him, said ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ without saying "from such-and-such," but left it unrestricted, because the absolute form is more eloquent in condemnation: the mind wanders in every direction, so it includes everything the context can bear. Also, omitting the complement implies generality, as is established in the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayan*). The meaning is that the competition for more has diverted you from everything that you are obliged to be occupied with, such as obedience to Allah and working for the Hereafter.

He described their death as visiting the graves because the dead has gone to his grave, just as the visitor goes to the place he visits. This is according to the view of those who say that the meaning of ﴿you visited the graves﴾ is "you died." It was also said that they used to visit the graves, saying, "This is the grave of so-and-so, and this is the grave of so-and-so," boasting by that.

﴿No! You will come to know﴾ is a restraint and rebuke for them from competing for more, and an alert that they will come to know the consequence of that on the Day of Resurrection, and it contains a severe threat.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the matter is not as you are, in competing for more and boasting.

Al-Farra' said: this repetition is for emphasis and intensification.

Mujahid said: it is a threat after a threat.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said likewise.

Al-Akhfash said: the estimate is: "If you knew with certain knowledge, you would not be distracted."

Then he repeated the warning and threat for emphasis, saying ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾. That is: then you will surely see the Blazing Fire with the sight that is the very essence of certainty, which is direct witnessing and beholding. It was also said the meaning is: you will surely see the Blazing Fire with your eyes from afar, then you will surely see it up close in direct witnessing.

It was also said that the first refers to seeing it before entering it, and the second to seeing it at the moment of entering.

It was also said that it is information about the continuance of their stay in the Fire, that is: it is a continuous, unbroken sight.

It was also said the meaning is: if you knew today with certain knowledge while you are in this world, you would surely see the Blazing Fire with the eye of your hearts, which is to imagine the matter of the Resurrection and its terrors.

Qatadah said: it refers to the disbelievers of Mecca, who were in good and blessing in this world, so they will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about thanking for what they had, and they did not thank the Lord of blessings, since they worshipped other than Him and associated partners with Him.

Al-Hasan said: only the people of the Fire will be questioned about the bliss.

It was also said the questioning is about security and health; it was said about health and leisure; it was said about perception through the senses; it was said about the delights of food and drink; it was said about cold drink and the shade of dwellings; it was said about moderation of temperament; it was said about the pleasure of sleep. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾, meaning from obedience, ﴿until you visited the graves﴾, meaning until death comes to you, ﴿No! Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Iyad ibn Ghanm, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Muslim and the authors of the Sunan collections (Ahl al-Sunan) and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went out and found Abu Bakr and Umar, and he said: 'What brought you out of your houses at this hour?' So they stood with him, and he came to a man from the Ansar, but he was not in his house. When his wife saw him, she said: 'Welcome.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Where is so-and-so?' Then he said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, it is equal to a thousand verses."

In another wording: "while ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ had just been revealed to him, and he was saying: 'The son of Adam says: My wealth, my wealth. Do you have any of your wealth except what you have eaten and consumed?'"

Muslim and others narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, without mentioning the recitation of this surah or its revelation, with the wording: "The servant says: My wealth, my wealth. Of his wealth he has only three things: what he eats and consumes, what he wears and wears out, or what he gives in charity and preserves. Everything else is gone, and he leaves it to the people."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated, and al-Bayhaqi weakened it, from Jarir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to us: "I am going to recite to you the surah ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾. Whoever weeps will have Paradise." He recited it, and some of us wept and some did not. Those who did not weep said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have striven hard to weep but could not." He said: "I will recite it to you a second time. Whoever weeps will have Paradise, and whoever cannot weep should feign weeping."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying: ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ means: the competition for more in wealth and children, boasting about their abundance, and vying with one another in them has preoccupied you.

It is said: *alhahu 'an kadha* (ألهاه عن كذا) and *alhahu* (ألهاه), meaning: when it occupied him. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*So I diverted her from the one with amulets, a suckling child.*

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of *alhakum* (ألهاكم) is: it made you forget.

﴿Until you visited the graves﴾ means: until death overtook you while you were in that state.

Qatadah said: the competition for more is boasting about tribes and clans.

Al-Dahhak said: *alhakum* means preoccupation with livelihood.

Muqatil and Qatadah also, and others, said: it was revealed concerning the Jews when they said, "We are more numerous than the sons of so-and-so, and the sons of so-and-so are more numerous than the sons of so-and-so." That preoccupied them until they died.

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning two clans of Quraysh: the Banu Abd Manaf and the Banu Sahm. They competed and vied in mastery and nobility in Islam. Each clan said: "We are more numerous in leadership, mightier in might, greater in men, and more numerous in commanders." The Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered the Banu Sahm, then they competed in the dead, and so the Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered them with their dead. So ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ was revealed, ﴿until you visited the graves﴾, boasting of the dead.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the Ansar.

*Al-Maqabir* (المقابر) is the plural of *maqbarah* (مقبرة), with the *ba'* vocalized either with a fatha or a damma.

The verse is evidence that preoccupation with worldly life, competing for more in it, and boasting in it are blameworthy traits. He, glory be to Him, said ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ without saying "from such-and-such," but left it unrestricted, because the absolute form is more eloquent in condemnation: the mind wanders in every direction, so it includes everything the context can bear. Also, omitting the complement implies generality, as is established in the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayan*). The meaning is that the competition for more has diverted you from everything that you are obliged to be occupied with, such as obedience to Allah and working for the Hereafter.

He described their death as visiting the graves because the dead has gone to his grave, just as the visitor goes to the place he visits. This is according to the view of those who say that the meaning of ﴿you visited the graves﴾ is "you died." As for the view of those who say that the meaning of ﴿you visited the graves﴾ is "you remembered the dead and counted them for boasting and competing," it is then in the manner of mockery toward them. It was also said that they used to visit the graves, saying, "This is the grave of so-and-so, and this is the grave of so-and-so," boasting by that.

﴿No! You will come to know﴾ is a restraint and rebuke for them from competing for more, and an alert that they will come to know the consequence of that on the Day of Resurrection, and it contains a severe threat.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the matter is not as you are, in competing for more and boasting.

Then he repeated the restraint, rebuke and threat, saying: ﴿Then no! You will come to know﴾. *Thumma* (ثم) here indicates that the second is more forceful than the first. It was said that the first is at death or in the grave, and the second is on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Farra' said: this repetition is for emphasis and intensification.

Mujahid said: it is a threat after a threat.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said likewise.

﴿No! If you knew with certainty of certainty﴾ means: if you knew with certain knowledge the matter to which you are returning, like your knowledge of what is certain to you in this world. The answer to *law* (لو) is omitted, meaning: that would have occupied you from competing for more and boasting, or you would have done what benefits you of good and left what does not benefit you of what you are engaged in. *Kalla* (كلا) in this third position is for restraint and rebuke, like the first two positions.

Al-Farra' said: it means "truly." It was also said that it means "unquestionably" in all three positions (*alla* (ألا)).

Qatadah said: the certainty here is death. It is also narrated from him that he said: it is resurrection.

Al-Akhfash said: the estimate is: "If you knew with certain knowledge, you would not be distracted."

His saying ﴿You will surely see the Blazing Fire﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and it contains further warning and threat. That is: By Allah, you will surely see the Blazing Fire in the Hereafter.

Al-Razi said: this is not the answer to *law*, because the answer to *law* is negated and this is affirmed, and because the following clause is joined to it: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned on that Day about the bliss﴾, which is future and must occur. He said: omitting the answer to *law* is common. The address is to the disbelievers, and it was said it is general, as in His saying ﴿And there is not one of you but will pass over it﴾ [Maryam: 71].

The majority read *latarawunna* (لترَوُنَّ) with a fatha on the *ta'*, in the active voice. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Amir read it with a damma, in the passive voice.

Then he repeated the warning and threat for emphasis, saying ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾. That is: then you will surely see the Blazing Fire with the sight that is the very essence of certainty, which is direct witnessing and beholding. It was also said the meaning is: you will surely see the Blazing Fire with your eyes from afar, then you will surely see it up close in direct witnessing.

It was also said that the first refers to seeing it before entering it, and the second to seeing it at the moment of entering.

It was also said that it is information about the continuance of their stay in the Fire, that is: it is a continuous, unbroken sight.

It was also said the meaning is: if you knew today with certain knowledge while you are in this world, you would surely see the Blazing Fire with the eye of your hearts, which is to imagine the matter of the Resurrection and its terrors.

﴿Then you will surely be questioned on that Day about the bliss﴾ means: about the bliss of this world that preoccupied you from working for the Hereafter.

Qatadah said: it refers to the disbelievers of Mecca, who were in good and blessing in this world, so they will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about thanking for what they had, and they did not thank the Lord of blessings, since they worshipped other than Him and associated partners with Him.

Al-Hasan said: only the people of the Fire will be questioned about the bliss.

Qatadah said: Allah, glory be to Him, will question every possessor of a blessing about what He bestowed upon him. This is the apparent meaning, and there is no basis for restricting the bliss to a single type or category, since its definite form indicates the genus or the totality. Mere questioning does not necessitate punishing the one questioned about the blessing he is asked about. Allah may question the believer about the blessings He bestowed upon him: how he spent them and what he did with them, so that he may know his shortcoming and his failure to perform the thanks that were obligatory upon him. It was also said the questioning is about security and health; it was said about health and leisure; it was said about perception through the senses; it was said about the delights of food and drink; it was said about cold drink and the shade of dwellings; it was said about moderation of temperament; it was said about the pleasure of sleep. Do you have any of your wealth except what you have eaten and consumed?'"

Muslim and others narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, without mentioning the recitation of this surah or its revelation, with the wording: "The servant says: My wealth, my wealth. Of his wealth he has only three things: what he eats and consumes, what he wears and wears out, or what he gives in charity and preserves. Everything else is gone, and he leaves it to the people."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated, and al-Bayhaqi weakened it, from Jarir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to us: "I am going to recite to you the surah ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾. Whoever weeps will have Paradise." He recited it, and some of us wept and some did not. Those who did not weep said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have striven hard to weep but could not." He said: "I will recite it to you a second time. Whoever weeps will have Paradise, and whoever cannot weep should feign weeping."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying: ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ means: the competition for more in wealth and children, boasting about their abundance, and vying with one another in them has preoccupied you.

It is said: *alhahu 'an kadha* (ألهاه عن كذا) and *alhahu* (ألهاه), meaning: when it occupied him. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*So I diverted her from the one with amulets, a suckling child.*

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of *alhakum* (ألهاكم) is: it made you forget.

﴿Until you visited the graves﴾ means: until death overtook you while you were in that state.

Qatadah said: the competition for more is boasting about tribes and clans.

Al-Dahhak said: *alhakum* means preoccupation with livelihood.

Muqatil and Qatadah also, and others, said: it was revealed concerning the Jews when they said, "We are more numerous than the sons of so-and-so, and the sons of so-and-so are more numerous than the sons of so-and-so." That preoccupied them until they died.

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning two clans of Quraysh: the Banu Abd Manaf and the Banu Sahm. They competed and vied in mastery and nobility in Islam. Each clan said: "We are more numerous in leadership, mightier in might, greater in men, and more numerous in commanders." The Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered the Banu Sahm, then they competed in the dead, and so the Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered them with their dead. So ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ was revealed, ﴿until you visited the graves﴾, boasting of the dead.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning two clans of the Ansar.

*Al-Maqabir* (المقابر) is the plural of *maqbarah* (مقبرة), with the *ba'* vocalized either with a fatha or a damma.

The verse is evidence that preoccupation with worldly life, competing for more in it, and boasting in it are blameworthy traits. He, glory be to Him, said ﴿Your preoccupation with competing for more has diverted you﴾ without saying "from such-and-such," but left it unrestricted, because the absolute form is more eloquent in condemnation: the mind wanders in every direction, so it includes everything the context can bear. Also, omitting the complement implies generality, as is established in the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayan*). The meaning is that the competition for more has diverted you from everything that you are obliged to be occupied with, such as obedience to Allah and working for the Hereafter.

He described their death as visiting the graves because the dead has gone to his grave, just as the visitor goes to the place he visits. This is according to the view of those who say that the meaning of ﴿you visited the graves﴾ is "you died." As for the view of those who say that the meaning of ﴿you visited the graves﴾ is "you remembered the dead and counted them for boasting and competing," it is then in the manner of mockery toward them. It was also said that they used to visit the graves, saying, "This is the grave of so-and-so, and this is the grave of so-and-so," boasting by that.

﴿No! You will come to know﴾ is a restraint and rebuke for them from competing for more, and an alert that they will come to know the consequence of that on the Day of Resurrection, and it contains a severe threat.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the matter is not as you are, in competing for more and boasting.

Then he repeated the restraint, rebuke and threat, saying: ﴿Then no! You will come to know﴾. *Thumma* (ثم) here indicates that the second is more forceful than the first. It was said that the first is at death or in the grave, and the second is on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Farra' said: this repetition is for emphasis and intensification.

Mujahid said: it is a threat after a threat.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said likewise.

﴿No! If you knew with certainty of certainty﴾ means: if you knew with certain knowledge the matter to which you are returning, like your knowledge of what is certain to you in this world. The answer to *law* (لو) is omitted, meaning: that would have occupied you from competing for more and boasting, or you would have done what benefits you of good and left what does not benefit you of what you are engaged in. *Kalla* (كلا) in this third position is for restraint and rebuke, like the first two positions.

Al-Farra' said: it means "truly." It was also said that it means "unquestionably" in all three positions (*alla* (ألا)).

Qatadah said: the certainty here is death. It is also narrated from him that he said: it is resurrection.

Al-Akhfash said: the estimate is: "If you knew with certain knowledge, you would not be distracted."

His saying ﴿You will surely see the Blazing Fire﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and it contains further warning and threat. That is: By Allah, you will surely see the Blazing Fire in the Hereafter.

Al-Razi said: this is not the answer to *law*, because the answer to *law* is negated and this is affirmed, and because the following clause is joined to it: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned on that Day about the bliss﴾, which is future and must occur. Then he repeated the warning and threat for emphasis, saying ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾. That is: then you will surely see the Blazing Fire with the sight that is the very essence of certainty, which is direct witnessing and beholding. It was also said the meaning is: you will surely see the Blazing Fire with your eyes from afar, then you will surely see it up close in direct witnessing.

It was also said that the first refers to seeing it before entering it, and the second to seeing it at the moment of entering.

It was also said that it is information about the continuance of their stay in the Fire, that is: it is a continuous, unbroken sight.

It was also said the meaning is: if you knew today with certain knowledge while you are in this world, you would surely see the Blazing Fire with the eye of your hearts, which is to imagine the matter of the Resurrection and its terrors.

﴿Then you will surely be questioned on that Day about the bliss﴾ means: about the bliss of this world that preoccupied you from working for the Hereafter.

Qatadah said: it refers to the disbelievers of Mecca, who were in good and blessing in this world, so they will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about thanking for what they had, and they did not thank the Lord of blessings, since they worshipped other than Him and associated partners with Him.

Al-Hasan said: only the people of the Fire will be questioned about the bliss.

Qatadah said: Allah, glory be to Him, will question every possessor of a blessing about what He bestowed upon him. This is the apparent meaning, and there is no basis for restricting the bliss to a single type or category, since its definite form indicates the genus or the totality. Mere questioning does not necessitate punishing the one questioned about the blessing he is asked about. Allah may question the believer about the blessings He bestowed upon him: how he spent them and what he did with them, so that he may know his shortcoming and his failure to perform the thanks that were obligatory upon him. It was also said the questioning is about security and health; it was said about health and leisure; it was said about perception through the senses; it was said about the delights of food and drink; it was said about cold drink and the shade of dwellings; it was said about moderation of temperament; it was said about the pleasure of sleep. The most appropriate is generality, as we have mentioned.

Al-Razi said: this is not the answer to *law*, because the answer to *law* is negated and this is affirmed, and because the following clause is joined to it: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned on that Day about the bliss﴾, which is future and must occur. He said: omitting the answer to *law* is common. The address is to the disbelievers, and it was said it is general, as in His saying ﴿And there is not one of you but will pass over it﴾ [Maryam: 71].

The majority read *latarawunna* (لترَوُنَّ) with a fatha on the *ta'*, in the active voice. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Amir read it with a damma, in the passive voice.

Then he repeated the warning and threat for emphasis, saying ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾. That is: then you will surely see the Blazing Fire with the sight that is the very essence of certainty, which is direct witnessing and beholding. It was also said the meaning is: you will surely see the Blazing Fire with your eyes from afar, then you will surely see it up close in direct witnessing.

It was also said that the first refers to seeing it before entering it, and the second to seeing it at the moment of entering.

It was also said that it is information about the continuance of their stay in the Fire, that is: it is a continuous, unbroken sight.

It was also said the meaning is: if you knew today with certain knowledge while you are in this world, you would surely see the Blazing Fire with the eye of your hearts, which is to imagine the matter of the Resurrection and its terrors.

Qatadah said: it refers to the disbelievers of Mecca, who were in good and blessing in this world, so they will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about thanking for what they had, and they did not thank the Lord of blessings, since they worshipped other than Him and associated partners with Him.

Al-Hasan said: only the people of the Fire will be questioned about the bliss.

Qatadah said: Allah, glory be to Him, will question every possessor of a blessing about what He bestowed upon him. This is the apparent meaning, and there is no basis for restricting the bliss to a single type or category, since its definite form indicates the genus or the totality. Mere questioning does not necessitate punishing the one questioned about the blessing he is asked about. Allah may question the believer about the blessings He bestowed upon him: how he spent them and what he did with them, so that he may know his shortcoming and his failure to perform the thanks that were obligatory upon him. It was also said the questioning is about security and health; it was said about health and leisure; it was said about perception through the senses; it was said about the delights of food and drink; it was said about cold drink and the shade of dwellings; it was said about moderation of temperament; it was said about the pleasure of sleep. Qatadah said: the competition for more is boasting about tribes and clans.

*Al-Maqabir* (المقابر) is the plural of *maqbarah* (مقبرة), with the *ba'* vocalized either with a fatha or a damma.

The meaning is that the competition for more has diverted you from everything that you are obliged to be occupied with, such as obedience to Allah and working for the Hereafter.
